Does π0 Look at the Object, or Remember the Place?

A failure analysis of a vision-language-action policy on LIBERO-Object, and why a high benchmark score can hide a memorized motion.

Ashzaeen Fatmi KhanResearch Assistant, Robotic Vision LaboratoryUniversity of Texas at Arlington
Dr. William BeksiFaculty AdvisorRobotic Vision Laboratory
Dr. Zongyao LyuGraduate MentorRobotic Vision Laboratory
Read the AbstractBrowse the LibraryView Code and Data
Contents Abstract 1 · Why This Question Matters 2 · Experimental Design 3 · Results 3.1 A Silent Bug 3.2 Image Changes 3.3 State Noise 3.4 Attention 3.5 Scene Changes 3.6 Putting It Together 4 · What I Built 5 · What This Demonstrates 6 · Threats to Validity 7 · Next Steps Glossary References

Abstract

In Plain EnglishA robot AI passes a standard test about 87 times out of 100. I checked whether it does that by seeing the object or by remembering where things usually are. The evidence says remembering.

Vision-language-action (VLA) policies map camera images and a natural-language instruction directly to robot actions. I study π0, a flow-matching VLA, on LIBERO-Object, where it succeeds in 84–94% of episodes. That score is consistent with two different mechanisms: grounding the instructed object in the scene, or replaying a learned trajectory from a familiar position.

I separate them with single-factor perturbations of the image (brightness, contrast), the proprioceptive state (injected noise), and the scene itself (swapping and displacing objects). Photometric changes leave success within 72–97%. A few centimeters of state noise collapses it to 4%, and swapping the target with a distractor takes it from 80% to 0 of 20, with the robot grasping the decoy in 60% of episodes. The evidence favors a state-anchored, position-keyed policy over visual grounding, and shows that the benchmark’s fixed six-slot layout cannot tell the two apart.

1

Why This Question Matters

A benchmark score is only as informative as the set of mechanisms that could produce it.

Why It MattersIn a home or a warehouse, objects are never exactly where they were last time. Whether a system succeeds by understanding or by habit decides whether it holds up.

LIBERO-Object asks a policy to pick up one of ten grocery items and place it in a basket. A policy that localizes the instructed object will pass. So will one that has learned a different rule: from this starting pose, execute this trajectory.

Picture someone who takes a mug from the same shelf every day. If the mug moves, a person who looks finds it, and a person on autopilot reaches for the empty spot. On a day when nothing moves, the two are indistinguishable. A benchmark where objects almost never move cannot separate them either.

Hypothesis One

Visual Grounding

The policy conditions its actions on where the instructed object appears in the image, and corrects as the scene changes.

Hypothesis Two

Trajectory Replay

The policy conditions on the robot’s own state and a memorized location, and replays a motion that worked in training.

The two predict the same score while objects sit where they did in training. They diverge when the scene, the robot state, or the camera changes. That divergence is what I measure. I organized the work around four candidate shortcuts (position, state, language and trajectory); the experiments below build direct evidence for position and state, and leave language untested.

2

Experimental Design

System Under Test

In Plain EnglishThe robot AI is a large neural network. It reads a camera image and a sentence, then outputs arm movements, many times per second.

π0 pairs a PaliGemma vision-language backbone with a separate 300M-parameter action expert that uses conditional flow matching to emit continuous action chunks at up to 50 Hz, for 4.03 billion parameters in total. The benchmark is LIBERO-Object: ten pick-and-place tasks with 50 provided initial states each. Every condition below runs 100 episodes (10 tasks × 10 trials) unless noted.

Infrastructure

Two processes communicate over HTTP: a policy server that loads π0 and serves predictions, and a simulator client that steps LIBERO and records success, video and per-step attention for every episode. They ran on a shared lab server with two A40 GPUs, in a pinned environment (transformers 5.3.0, torch 2.7.1, Python 3.12).

Four Stages

Stage 1Groundwork

Literature review and a plan agreed with my advisor and mentor.

May – June
Stage 2Trusted Baseline

Rebuilt the lab pipeline and traced why it scored 10 of 100.

June – July
Stage 3Perturb the Inputs

Brightness, contrast and state noise. About 2,700 episodes.

July
Stage 4Perturb the Scene

Swap and move objects, tracking what the robot touches.

August

Three Design Rules

Single-Factor Changes

Each sweep varies one variable with the seed fixed, so a result points at a cause.

No-Op Controls

One condition runs the full pipeline but changes nothing. If it misses the baseline, my own harness is broken.

Attention as Hypothesis

Where the model attends is a clue to test, not proof. A claim counts only after a perturbation confirms it.

What I Measure

Success rate against the clean baseline. For attention, the last layer’s action-query attention over the 256 base-camera and 256 wrist-camera patch tokens, reshaped into 16×16 maps and summarized by peak value, entropy, Gini coefficient and top-5 patch share. In the scene experiments, I also record which object the robot actually disturbed.

3

Results

Five findings, in the order I found them. Figures 2, 3, 5 and 7 are interactive.

3.1A Silent Dependency Bug

In Plain EnglishA software version mix-up had quietly scrambled part of the robot’s vision. No error message, just a score of 10 out of 100.

The pipeline I inherited scored 10 of 100 and raised no error. The checkpoint’s SigLIP vision encoder is named differently across transformers releases, so under 5.12.1 most of the vision tower loaded with random initialization while appearing to load correctly. The policy was effectively reaching from memory. Pinning 5.3.0 restored all 4.03 billion parameters with zero missing weights and lifted success to 91. A clean run, with the inherited brightness offset removed, settled at 87.

That 87 is the anchor for every later comparison, and the reason the project carries a version pin and a no-op control.

3.2Image Changes Barely Register

Brightness offsets from 0 to 100 held success between 86% and 96%. Contrast gains from 0.2× to 2.0× held it between 72% and 97%, and the most degraded image (77 of 100) is statistically indistinguishable from the clean one (84 of 100). A plausible reading is that the encoder normalizes away affine intensity changes. Either way, two independent ways of badly degrading the image did not move the score, which sits poorly with a policy that depends on what it sees.

3.3State Noise Collapses Success

In Plain EnglishThe robot keeps an internal estimate of where its arm is. I corrupted that estimate slightly and left the camera alone. The robot followed its corrupted estimate, not what its camera showed.

The robot state is eight-dimensional (end-effector position, orientation and gripper), and its dimensions have different units. I injected zero-mean Gaussian noise per dimension, scaled by a fixed physical reference vector, so one multiplier σ sweeps a comparable magnitude everywhere; σ = 1 is about 2 cm of position noise. The camera image was never touched.

If π0 closed the loop visually, a few centimeters of state error would be recoverable from the intact camera stream, and success would degrade gradually. It collapses instead: more than half the attempts fail by 2 cm and nearly all by 4 cm. Failing episodes still show a confident, smooth reach, just toward a displaced location, which is what a replayed trajectory would do.

3.4Attention Does Not Explain Behavior

I rendered attention maps for ten episodes of each of four objects on the clean baseline. They did not line up with success:

ObjectWhere Peak Attention LandedOutcome
Alphabet SoupThe far background band, in 10 of 10 episodesSucceeds 10/10
Orange JuiceSharp and confident, but on a neighboring bottle, in 10 of 10 episodesSucceeds 10/10
Chocolate PuddingDiffuse; almost nothing on the wrist cameraSucceeds about 8/10
MilkSplit between two hotspots in the failuresFails 2/10

The dissociation also runs both ways. Under state noise, attention statistics were identical between a successful clean rollout and its failing noisy counterparts, while behavior collapsed. Under contrast changes, top-5 patch share rose from 44% to 99%, a tenfold swing in sharpness, while success stayed flat. Task success did not track the attention pattern in either direction.

3.5Scene Changes Break the Policy

Before changing anything, I decoded every object’s pose across all ten tasks and fifty initial states. LIBERO-Object is extremely regular: every task places objects on the same six (x, y) slots, positional randomization is at most 2 cm, and the target always occupies one of only two slots.

A policy that ignores language and vision and simply reaches for one of two memorized points therefore has a structural route to a high score. That does not prove π0 does so, but it means the benchmark alone cannot separate grounding from memorization. So I rewrote the scene itself, editing the object poses in the simulator’s initial state, and tracked which object the robot touched:

  • Swap the target with a distractor: success fell from 80% to 0 of 20. In 60% of episodes the robot grasped the decoy now occupying the target’s usual slot, and it touched the true target in only 15%.
  • Displace only the target by 5 cm: success fell to 10%. The response is a cliff, not a slope.
  • Displace everything else by up to 15 cm: success stayed at 85–100%. This control matters: it rules out “π0 dislikes any rearranged scene” and shows the policy keys on where the target used to be.

Explore Every Condition. Each attempt below is one of 20 episodes (10 tasks, 2 attempts each). The clip shows the same task, picking up the ketchup, wherever one is embedded.

3.6Putting It Together

EvidenceObservationPoints To
State Noise86% falls to 4% at about 4 cm, with the camera intactA state-anchored trajectory
Attention AuditSharp but often misplaced, and decoupled from success both waysVision is not driving the action
Scene RearrangementSwap takes 80% to 0 of 20; 60% of grasps land on the decoyA position-keyed shortcut

The policy appears to go to the right place with the right motion, not to the right object.

This also fits the spring study I presented as a poster at the CRA Undergraduate Conference: the model tolerated moved objects but struggled when the robot or camera was moved, which is what an arm-anchored policy would do.

4

What I Built

The findings are only as good as the experiments, so I built the experiments to be rerun.

InfrastructureA Reproducible Pipeline

A model server and simulator client that record every episode from a pinned environment. I documented the version pin behind the silent bug.

ToolingA Single-Factor Sweep Driver

Varies exactly one setting across a list of values with all else fixed, and writes a per-condition summary. It produced the brightness, contrast and state-noise results.

ToolingA Scene Perturbation System

Swaps and moves objects by rewriting simulator initial states, validates that placements settle physically, and records which object the robot disturbed.

AnalysisAttention Metrics

Turns where the model attends into 16×16 maps and four per-frame statistics, so it can be measured rather than eyeballed.

OperationsA Shared-GPU Watcher

Frees the lab’s shared server after a long run finishes cleanly, and leaves it up for inspection if the run crashed.

DocumentationAn Organized Public Repository

Code, weekly reports, charts, data tables, 160 clips and guides under an MIT license.

5

What This Work Demonstrates

Root-Causing Silent Failures

Traced a 10-of-100 score to one library version that broke the model without an error, and documented the fix.

Experimental Design

Single-factor sweeps, fixed seeds, no-op controls and a control that rules out the obvious objection.

Reusable Tooling

A sweep driver, a scene system, analysis code and run scripts, with guides and a license.

Care With Shared Resources

Wrote the GPU watcher after a shared server was left running, so it cannot recur.

Communication at Several Levels

Fifteen weekly reports, a technical report, a plain-language summary, a presentation, and this brief.

Honesty About Uncertainty

Every claim is paired with its limits, and my reports flag results I have not yet verified.

6

Threats to Validity

  • One model, one benchmark. Results are for π0 on LIBERO-Object and do not show that other VLA models behave the same way.
  • The newest results are the thinnest. The scene experiments use 20 episodes per condition and scripts written from scratch; they need independent review.
  • Attention is a diagnostic, not proof. I have not yet recorded it during the swap, so I cannot say whether it follows the target to its new slot.
  • Run-to-run variance. The clean baseline came out at 84%, 86% and 87% across runs, and each sweep used a single seed, so gaps near 4 points are noise.
  • State leaks into the wrist camera. The gripper is visible to it, so a small drop under state noise does not alone prove the policy ignores state.
  • Some figures were transcribed from my weekly reports instead of regenerated from raw logs, which stay on the lab server.
7

Next Steps

  • Record attention during the swap, to test whether it follows the target while the action goes to the old slot.
  • Classify when each failure occurs (approach, grasp, transport or placement).
  • Add a frozen-state control, and test whether the wording of the instruction matters.
  • Evaluate on benchmarks with genuine position randomization, which breaks the object-to-location correlation.

Glossary

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Model

A neural network that takes camera images and a written instruction and outputs robot actions. π0 (“pi-zero”) is one from Physical Intelligence.

Benchmark

A shared test for comparing AI systems. LIBERO is a suite of simulated robot tasks; LIBERO-Object has ten pick-and-place tasks.

Proprioception

The robot’s internal estimate of its own joint and gripper positions, independent of the cameras.

Closed-Loop Visual Servoing

Continually correcting a robot’s motion using what its camera sees, so that errors get fixed as they occur.

Attention Map

A heat map of which input patches a transformer weighs most when producing an output. A useful clue about what a model uses, not proof.

No-Op Control

A condition that executes all of the perturbation code but changes nothing, used to confirm the harness itself introduces no effect.

Shortcut

A learned rule that earns the right answer on a test without the understanding the test was designed to measure.

Episode and Success Rate

One attempt at a task is an episode. A success rate of 87/100 means 87 of 100 episodes put the right object in the basket.

References

  1. Physical Intelligence. π0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control. arXiv:2410.24164, 2024.
  2. Liu, B., et al. LIBERO: Benchmarking Knowledge Transfer in Lifelong Robot Learning. NeurIPS 36, 2023.
  3. LIBERO-PRO: Towards Robust and Fair Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Models Beyond Memorization.

How the Footage Is Organized

One clip is one episode, filmed from a front camera at 256×256. The object-moving experiments produced 160 clips: 8 conditions × 20 episodes. The file name carries the outcome, so ep00-fail-ketchup.mp4 reads as episode 0, failed, task “pick up the ketchup and place it in the basket.”

scene-perturbation-clips/
├── move-target/                    only the target is displaced
│   ├── 0cm-no-op/                  no-op control               16/20
│   ├── 5cm/                        5 cm                         2/20
│   ├── 10cm/                       10 cm                        1/20
│   └── 15cm/                       15 cm                        0/20
├── move-distractors/               everything except the target is displaced
│   ├── 5cm/                        20/20
│   ├── 10cm/                       19/20
│   └── 15cm/                       17/20
└── swap-target-and-distractor/     target and a distractor exchange slots   0/20
